MURDER BY MARKETPLACE

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When marketplace turns to murder.

Unique Selling Point:
In South Africa today, a man trying to sell his phone to pay for his wedding can end up in a coffin, and a child can stare down the barrel of a gun.


Summary:
He invited them to a wedding. They came to a funeral.
29-year-old Mogamat Yusuf Daniels should have been a groom. Instead, days before the ceremony, he was executed in a Facebook Marketplace ambush in Ottery.
Two young women lured him under the guise of buying his iPhone. His fiancée had been with him just half an hour earlier. Yusuf took his cousin and the cousin’s child along for safety.

But safety was a lie.
When they arrived, the gunman stepped from the shadows, shoved his weapon against the boy’s head, and demanded everything.
Yusuf drew his licensed firearm to protect the child. Shots cracked through the night. Moments later, he lay dead on the ground - a groom-to-be bleeding out in front of a terrified child.

This isn’t random. It’s part of a new criminal economy built on Facebook Marketplace:
In Winterveldt, a man was hijacked and locked in the boot of his own car.
In Midrand, a fake sale ended in a police gun battle - five suspects shot, others fled.
In Pretoria, five more were arrested in another syndicate sting, young women again used as bait.

The blueprint is the same: lure, misdirect, test the goods, then ambush.
A digital platform has become South Africa’s deadliest street corner.

The investigation: Carte Blanche exposes the anatomy of these traps - how syndicates use women to bait, children to break victims’ resolve, and trust itself as the weapon.
We’ll confront SAPS on why they only arrive after the body bags, and demand answers from Meta, whose platform has been weaponised into a marketplace of death.

Press Release:


Marketplace Murder
He was ready to be married; instead, he was buried. This week, a 29-year-old man was executed in an armed robbery in Ottery, Western Cape. It’s not an isolated tragedy: it’s part of a new criminal economy built on Facebook Marketplace. A man hijacked and locked in the boot of his own car. A fake sale ending in a police gun battle. The blueprint is the same: lure, misdirect, test the goods, then ambush. Carte Blanche exposes the anatomy of a trap, asks why police often arrive after the body bags, and demands answers from the digital platform that’s become South Africa’s deadliest street corner.
Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


MURDER BY MARKETPLACE: FINAL:

(MACFARLANE): “September 24th, 9:20pm. Mogamat Yusuf Daniels believes he’s closing a Facebook Marketplace deal. The buyers are already in his car.”
(MACFARLANE): “After a gunman opens fire, Mogamat is killed.”
(ZAINAB DANIELS):
“His eyes was open and I said ‘he still wanted to see his Mommy’. And I could see these tears in his eyes. I don’t have mercy for that people.”

(MACFARLANE): “29-year-old Mogamat Yusuf was just a week away from getting married. He’d put his cell phone up for sale on Facebook Marketplace for R7 500 to help cover some of the costs.”
(MACFARLANE): “The buyer, a woman, offered to pay the full price.”
VOICENOTE 1 (BUYER):
“Do you think you are able to deliver for me please man? Because I don’t want to be on the road too late. But let me know, maybe I can reimburse you with petrol money or whatever the case may be.”
(MACFARLANE): “Mogamat took precautions. He dropped his fiancée at home and took his cousin and nephew along for the exchange. He also carried a gun.”
(MACFARLANE): “Then the location changed - from a petrol station to a deserted supermarket parking lot in Ottery, in Cape Town’s Southern Suburbs.”
VOICENOTE (BUYER):
“Listen, I got to the shop here by the Shia Mosque. I’m with my neighbour. So, so you can come here.”
(MACFARLANE): “The buyers were bait.”
(ABDURUGMAN JACOBS): “They were exchanging shots - so he shot Mogamat Yusuf…”
(MACFARLANE): “Yes…”
(ABDURAGMAN JACOBS): “…first, but Mogamat Yusuf kept on shooting.”
(MACFARLANE): “Returned fire, yes.”
(ANDURAGMAN JACOBS): “Returned fire.”
(MACFARLANE): “Abdurugman Jacobs is Mogamat’s uncle. He believes it was trust rather than carelessness that cost his nephew his life.”
(ABDURUGMAN JACOBS): “Mogamat know about the things that’s happening and that, but he was a trustworthy person, he had that with everyone.”

(MACFARLANE): “After the shooting, investigators traced the trail of bullets across Ottery’s streets.”
MACFARLANE LINK: “So these are some of the markings left by police from that fateful day. The entire area littered with shell casings as well as bullet holes. It shows that a real gun battle ensued here. A gun battle that Mogamat Yusuf, didn’t survive.”
(MACFARLANE): “One of the gunmen was shot and taken to hospital, and another suspect - a woman - was arrested. But the alleged mastermind - the woman who set the trap by posing as an interested buyer - is still on the run.”

(ZAINAB DANIELS): “They told me he’s, he’s at janazah, and I say to don’t talk nonsense, check, he is still alive, just check his pulse.’
(MACFARLANE): “The night her son was killed is frozen in Zainab Daniels’s memory.”
(ZAINAB DANIELS): “And then my son was in… he is gone, he is, he is gone - there was a pulse and there wasn’t a pulse, and I broke down.”
(MACFARLANE): “She remembers a boy who loved to chat, and brought her home to life.”
(ZAINAB DANIELS): “We talk, we speak, he always wanted me around speaking to him, teasing, grabbing me, kissing me, hugging, and he always said to me: ‘Shukran Mummy, shukran Mummy…’”
(MACFARLANE): “What will you miss most about him?”
(ZAINAB DANIELS): “Most what I miss most about him? Teasing. Teasing.”
(MACFARLANE): “So he was very playful.”
(ZAINAB DANIELS): “Very, jolly person, singing - he loved singing.”
MACFARLANE LINK:
“As a parent, you never think that you’ll ever bury your child. But it’s even worse when you find out that they’ve been brutally murdered. And it’s all because of a simple thing - like a cellphone.”

(MACFARLANE): “Facebook Marketplace is an online platform where users can buy, sell, and trade. It’s like a digital version of a local flea market. Crucially, while it does allow for shipping, buyers and sellers can also connect face-to-face.”

(MACFARLANE) ‘Was he aware of the dangers around Marketplace? Was he aware of some of the things that have been happening?”
(ZAINAB DANIELS): “No, he wasn’t really for Marketplace, I dunno what happened, what happened there. I just heard they said he cancelled this deal. But I think these girls was keeping on messaging him.”

(MACFARLANE): “According to the police’s Andre Traut, Mogamat’s murder isn’t an isolated case.”
(COL. ANDRE TRAUT): “A opportunistic criminal would walk past, he’ll see a cellphone lying on the table and grab it and run. That’s opportunistic. Here, you are targeted as the seller on a platform. You are being monitored, you’re been called, you’re been set up - and you’re be ambushed.”
(MACFARLANE): “Across the country, Facebook Marketplace deals are being hijacked - sellers lured into fake meetings that end in robbery, assault, and sometimes, death.”
(MACFARLANE): “To fight back, police have turned to undercover operations - replacing sellers with decoys to expose syndicates before they strike.”
(COL. ANDRE TRAUT): “If you feel that you are being set up into a, into a robbery, advise the police and we can do a clandestine operation, and send a police officer there and make the arrest. We’ve done that before.”
MACFARLANE LINK: “Police say they’re alarmed by the rise of these attacks, but their advice is blunt: don’t go alone, don’t go at night, and don’t go to any hidden places. And if the buyer refuses to go to a public place, it’s a trap.”

(MACFARLANE): “Two years ago, tattoo artist Noulen Basson thought he was buying a car part on Facebook Marketplace.”
(NOULEN BASSON): “The guy sent me a location, he told me I can come and pick it up, he was like ‘Hey buddy, you can come see me at my house.’ And he sounded like a nice guy…
(MACFARLANE): “So super friendly?”
(NOULEN BASSON): “Super friendly, sounded like a super nice guy.”
(MACFARLANE): “Instead, he and a friend walked into an ambush.”
(NOULEN BASSON): “On our way to the location he changed the location. And when we got to the new location that he sent me, I was met by a 17 year old that seemed like he was stressing, he was sweaty and he was hyperventilating... But the moment he stepped out of the car, everyone started rushing towards us. So this is about 12 people, I guess, probably around 12 - if it wasn’t more.”
(MACFARLANE): “Noulen and his friend fought back…”
(MACFARLANE): “…and managed to escape - but not before being robbed of their phones and cash.”
(MACFARLANE): “Afterwards, Noulen posted a video online showing a map of the ambush site. It was viewed over a million times and helped to expose a syndicate operating in an area called Browns Farm near Nyanga - a notorious crime hotspot in the Western Cape.”
(NOULEN BASSON): “A lot of people have messaged me and they’ve said because of this video they’ve been saved, or they've messaged me after they’ve been robbed or also been in a similar situation. I tattooed a guy that got shot in his neck by them…”
(MACFARLANE) ‘By the same crew?’
(NOULEN BASSON) “By the same, the same crew, it’s like a syndicate.”
(MACFARLANE): “Noulen walked away from an ambush. Mogamat Yusuf didn’t.”

(MACFARLANE): “His murder has exposed how a platform for doing business has become a hunting ground for criminals.”
(ANNA COLLARD): “So, uhm, there are a couple of reasons why the Facebook Marketplace is so attractive to criminals. One, obviously there’s lots of people there, so it’s a nice, big attack surface.”
(MACFARLANE): “Anna Collard is a cybersecurity psychologist.”
(ANNA COLLARD): “The second one is it’s relatively easy to set up fake accounts, and Facebook is - or Meta in general - they aren’t that great with taking down fake or fraudulent accounts. You know, it’s all about profits - the more accounts they have, the more advertising can be sold to those. So there’s no real intention or motivation to take down those scammy accounts.”

(MACFARLANE): “Have you seen patterns where we’re now starting to link sort of what’s happening on Marketplace to greater crime syndicates, you know where it now escalates to things like hijackings, extortion, kidnappings, and, and, and that sorts of things?”
(ANNA COLLARD): “100%. So what we have to remember is that the syndicates themselves - whether those are the human traffickers, the drug dealers, they’re all converging with the cybercrime world. So oftentimes, the Marketplace scams are sort of entry points, you know. They’ve caught on, and they’re also digitised, right.”
(MACFARLANE): “Anna says Meta, Facebook’s parent company, could do more to curb the criminality, but isn’t.”
(ANNA COLLARD): “Generally their response is below par; safety is not their priority, at the end of the day, so.”
(MACFARLANE): “But the company insists it’s tackling the problem.”
(MACFARLANE): “Meta told us that ‘bad actors’ target all online marketplaces, and Facebook is no exception. The company says it removes listings that violate its rules, bans sellers who abuse the platform, and urges users to check profiles, meet in safe public spaces, and report suspicious activity. Adding that it also works with law enforcement when required.”

(MACFARLANE): “So, while a multi-billion dollar company defends its platform, justice for Mogamat’s family can only come from the successful arrest and prosecution of the perpetrators.”
(ZAINAB DANIELS): “I don’t care what happened. No bail - no bail. They need to be punished, because he didn’t deserve to die like that.”

Was he aware of some of the things that have been happening?” (ZAINAB DANIELS): “No, he wasn’t really for Marketplace, I dunno what happened, what happened there. I just heard they said he cancelled this deal. But I think these girls was keeping on messaging him.” (MACFARLANE): “According to the police’s Andre Traut, Mogamat’s murder isn’t an isolated case.” (COL. ANDRE TRAUT): “A opportunistic criminal would walk past, he’ll see a cellphone lying on the table and grab it and run. That’s opportunistic. Here, you are targeted as the seller on a platform. You are being monitored, you’re been called, you’re been set up - and you’re be ambushed.” (MACFARLANE): “Across the country, Facebook Marketplace deals are being hijacked - sellers lured into fake meetings that end in robbery, assault, and sometimes, death.” (MACFARLANE): “To fight back, police have turned to undercover operations - replacing sellers with decoys to expose syndicates before they strike.” (COL. ANDRE TRAUT): “If you feel that you are being set up into a, into a robbery, advise the police and we can do a clandestine operation, and send a police officer there and make the arrest. We’ve done that before.” MACFARLANE LINK: “Police say they’re alarmed by the rise of these attacks, but their advice is blunt: don’t go alone, don’t go at night, and don’t go to any hidden places. And if the buyer refuses to go to a public place, it’s a trap.” (MACFARLANE): “Two years ago, tattoo artist Noulen Basson thought he was buying a car part on Facebook Marketplace.” (NOULEN BASSON): “The guy sent me a location, he told me I can come and pick it up, he was like ‘Hey buddy, you can come see me at my house.’ And he sounded like a nice guy… (MACFARLANE): “So super friendly?” (NOULEN BASSON): “Super friendly, sounded like a super nice guy.” (MACFARLANE): “Instead, he and a friend walked into an ambush.” (NOULEN BASSON): “On our way to the location he changed the location. And when we got to the new location that he sent me, I was met by a 17 year old that seemed like he was stressing, he was sweaty and he was hyperventilating... But the moment he stepped out of the car, everyone started rushing towards us. So this is about 12 people, I guess, probably around 12 - if it wasn’t more.” (MACFARLANE): “Noulen and his friend fought back…” (MACFARLANE): “…and managed to escape - but not before being robbed of their phones and cash.” (MACFARLANE): “Afterwards, Noulen posted a video online showing a map of the ambush site. It was viewed over a million times and helped to expose a syndicate operating in an area called Browns Farm near Nyanga - a notorious crime hotspot in the Western Cape.” (NOULEN BASSON): “A lot of people have messaged me and they’ve said because of this video they’ve been saved, or they've messaged me after they’ve been robbed or also been in a similar situation. I tattooed a guy that got shot in his neck by them…” (MACFARLANE) ‘By the same crew?’ (NOULEN BASSON) “By the same, the same crew, it’s like a syndicate.” (MACFARLANE): “Noulen walked away from an ambush. Mogamat Yusuf didn’t.” (MACFARLANE): “His murder has exposed how a platform for doing business has become a hunting ground for criminals.” (ANNA COLLARD): “So, uhm, there are a couple of reasons why the Facebook Marketplace is so attractive to criminals. One, obviously there’s lots of people there, so it’s a nice, big attack surface.” (MACFARLANE): “Anna Collard is a cybersecurity psychologist.” (ANNA COLLARD): “The second one is it’s relatively easy to set up fake accounts, and Facebook is - or Meta in general - they aren’t that great with taking down fake or fraudulent accounts. You know, it’s all about profits - the more accounts they have, the more advertising can be sold to those. So there’s no real intention or motivation to take down those scammy accounts.” (MACFARLANE): “Have you seen patterns where we’re now starting to link sort of what’s happening on Marketplace to greater crime syndicates, you know where it now escalates to things like hijackings, extortion, kidnappings, and, and, and that sorts of things?” (ANNA COLLARD): “100%. So what we have to remember is that the syndicates themselves - whether those are the human traffickers, the drug dealers, they’re all converging with the cybercrime world. So oftentimes, the Marketplace scams are sort of entry points, you know. They’ve caught on, and they’re also digitised, right.” (MACFARLANE): “Anna says Meta, Facebook’s parent company, could do more to curb the criminality, but isn’t.” (ANNA COLLARD): “Generally their response is below par; safety is not their priority, at the end of the day, so.” (MACFARLANE): “But the company insists it’s tackling the problem.” (MACFARLANE): “Meta told us that ‘bad actors’ target all online marketplaces, and Facebook is no exception. The company says it removes listings that violate its rules, bans sellers who abuse the platform, and urges users to check profiles, meet in safe public spaces, and report suspicious activity. Adding that it also works with law enforcement when required.” (MACFARLANE): “So, while a multi-billion dollar company defends its platform, justice for Mogamat’s family can only come from the successful arrest and prosecution of the perpetrators.” (ZAINAB DANIELS): “I don’t care what happened. No bail - no bail. They need to be punished, because he didn’t deserve to die like that.”

metadata.Unique Selling Point: In South Africa today, a man trying to sell his phone to pay for his wedding can end up in a coffin, and a child can stare down the barrel of a gun.
metadata.Summary: He invited them to a wedding. They came to a funeral. 29-year-old Mogamat Yusuf Daniels should have been a groom. Instead, days before the ceremony, he was executed in a Facebook Marketplace ambush in Ottery. Two young women lured him under the guise of buying his iPhone. His fiancée had been with him just half an hour earlier. Yusuf took his cousin and the cousin’s child along for safety. But safety was a lie. When they arrived, the gunman stepped from the shadows, shoved his weapon against the boy’s head, and demanded everything. Yusuf drew his licensed firearm to protect the child. Shots cracked through the night. Moments later, he lay dead on the ground - a groom-to-be bleeding out in front of a terrified child. This isn’t random. It’s part of a new criminal economy built on Facebook Marketplace: In Winterveldt, a man was hijacked and locked in the boot of his own car. In Midrand, a fake sale ended in a police gun battle - five suspects shot, others fled. In Pretoria, five more were arrested in another syndicate sting, young women again used as bait. The blueprint is the same: lure, misdirect, test the goods, then ambush. A digital platform has become South Africa’s deadliest street corner. The investigation: Carte Blanche exposes the anatomy of these traps - how syndicates use women to bait, children to break victims’ resolve, and trust itself as the weapon. We’ll confront SAPS on why they only arrive after the body bags, and demand answers from Meta, whose platform has been weaponised into a marketplace of death.
